## Filming locations to visit across Scotland

Bring your favourite stories to life at real places, arranged so you can explore Scotland one location at a time.

![Image 6: The Pass of Glencoe is a deep gorge cut by the River Coe and surrounded by towering mountains, geology and history.](https://www.visitscotland.com/binaries/content/gallery/visitscotland/cms-images/2023/02/17/pass-of-glencoe)

The Pass of Glencoe

© VisitScotland / Kenny Lam

### Drama in the Highlands

The Highlands have long been a favourite for directors thanks to their raw, cinematic presence. [Glencoe](https://www.visitscotland.com/places-to-go/glencoe) delivers brooding peaks and sweeping valleys that have appeared in _Braveheart_, _Skyfall_, _Outlaw King_, _Mary Queen of Scots_ and several _Harry Potter_ films, making it one of Scotland’s most recognisable on‑screen landscapes. Nearby [Glen Nevis](https://forestryandland.gov.scot/visit/glen-nevis) adds softer, greener stretches of Highland scenery that featured prominently in _Braveheart_. Remember, you can visit the Highlands year-round, and you’ll often find a quieter, more intimate experience in autumn and winter.

[Visit the Highlands](https://www.visitscotland.com/places-to-go/highlands)

![Image 7](https://www.visitscotland.com/binaries/content/gallery/visitscotland/cms-images/2022/07/04/doune-castle---outlander)

Doune Castle

© Sony Pictures Television 2014-2026, all rights reserved.

### Historic heartlands

Central Scotland is a popular setting for both period dramas and fantasy epics! [Doune Castle](https://www.historicenvironment.scot/visit-a-place/places/doune-castle/) alone has appeared as Castle Leoch in _Outlander_, Winterfell in the _Game of Thrones_ pilot and _Monty Python and the Holy Grail_, thanks to its imposing stone walls and preserved medieval features. Around [Stirling](https://www.visitscotland.com/places-to-go/stirling), dramatic battlements and rolling landscapes have supported countless adaptations rooted in Scottish history. New release _Glenrothan_, the directorial debut of acclaimed actor Brian Cox, has recently been filmed in[The Trossachs](https://www.visitscotland.com/places-to-go/national-parks/loch-lomond-trossachs).

[Find a Scottish castle](https://www.visitscotland.com/things-to-do/attractions/castles)

![Image 8](https://www.visitscotland.com/binaries/content/gallery/visitscotland/cms-images/2022/06/30/301/calton-hill-evening)

The Edinburgh skyline viewed from Calton Hill

© VisitScotland / Kenny Lam

### Edinburgh’s atmospheric streets

Edinburgh’s winding streets, gothic corners and historic closes lend themselves to stories with darker moods. Guillermo del Toro brought _Frankenstein_ to life here, using the city’s blend of architecture and ancient character. The capital also sets the scene for _Rebus_, grounding the detective in authentic neighbourhoods, classic pubs and old streets.

[Discover Edinburgh](https://www.visitscotland.com/places-to-go/edinburgh)

![Image 9](https://www.visitscotland.com/binaries/content/gallery/visitscotland/cms-images/2025/04/30/glasgow-city-centre-mural.jpg)

A mural by Smug depicts St Mungo and the tale of The Bird That Never Flew

© Glasgow Life

### Glasgow’s urban edge

Directors turn to Glasgow when they need scale, pace and architectural versatility. Its grid layout and mix of Victorian and modern streets allowed _World War Z_ to capture large crowd scenes right in the city centre. This layout makes it the perfect stand-in for American cities in films like _Batman_ and _Indiana Jones_. Its adaptable look continues to attract productions that want the punch of a big city without losing character.

[Visit Glasgow](https://www.visitscotland.com/places-to-go/glasgow)

![Image 10: Sunset colours at Findhorn Beach](https://www.visitscotland.com/binaries/content/gallery/visitscotland/cms-images/2024/10/21/sunset-colours-at-findhorn-beach)

Sunset colours at Findhorn Beach

© @alittlebitofclaire & @unlimitedscotland

### Legendary coastal scenes

Scotland’s coastline and clifftop fortresses are natural storytellers. [Dunnottar Castle](https://www.dunnottarcastle.co.uk/), perched on a rugged headland near Stonehaven, inspired the dramatic look of Disney Pixar’s _Brave_ with its towering cliffs and stormy silhouette.

Recently, Christopher Nolan’s _The Odyssey_ filmed on the Banffshire and Moray coast, centring on the dramatic clifftop ruins of Findlater Castle, where Nolan spent weeks capturing key scenes with a large cast and crew. Temporary sets rose above the Moray Firth, with nearby Buckie Harbour, Portsoy, Cullen, Sunnyside Beach, and Burghead also used for sequences involving replica ancient Greek ships and coastal battles.

[Enjoy Scotland’s beaches](https://www.visitscotland.com/things-to-do/landscapes-nature/beaches)

![Image 11](https://www.visitscotland.com/binaries/content/gallery/visitscotland/cms-images/2024/09/18/saoirse-ronan-in-the-outrun)

Saoirse Ronan in The Outrun

© StudioCanal

### Inspiring islands

Our gorgeous, windswept islands offer striking visual contrasts. [Orkney](https://www.visitscotland.com/places-to-go/islands/orkney) is central to _The Outrun_, where the islands' geology, wildlife and layered history shaped both the book and the production’s sense of place. Rugged quietness and open skies give directors room to craft intimate and mythic stories.

[Voyage to the islands](https://www.visitscotland.com/places-to-go/islands)

# Monty Python

## Monty Python and The Holy Grail Filming Locations in Scotland

Monty Python and The Holy Grail is a 1975 British comedy film that has become a cult classic over the years. The film is set in medieval England, but several of its **most memorable scenes were actually filmed in Scotland**.

The filmmakers chose Scotland because of its stunning landscapes and historic castles, which made the perfect backdrop in contract to the film's wacky characters and absurd humour.

**Fans of the film can still visit these locations and even recreate their favourite scenes.** In fact, you can join us on various tours around Scotland including a [**day tour to filming locations**](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/alnwick-castle-rosslyn-chapel-hogwarts-day-tour-from-edinburgh) (_Hogwarts from Harry Potter, New Asgard from the Avengers, Rosslyn Chapel from The Da Vinci Code and Leaderfoot Viaduct from Indiana Jones_).

Alternatively, [**check-out this day tour to Doune Castle**](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/outlander-doune-castle-loch-lomond-day-tour-from-glasgow) (_below: Castle of Guy de Lombar_) & more.

**Right, let’s jump into some of the locations from the film!**

[![Image 6: A stone castle viewed from a grassy landscape, surrounded by trees with leaves in the foreground.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5efb46cf46fb3d2f36091afa/4b260846-4294-4876-a614-1c9fcc49f6ca/Doune+Castle.jpg)](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/outlander-doune-castle-loch-lomond-day-tour-from-glasgow)

#### Castle Stalker

Name: From the Gaelic Word "Stalcaire" Meaning "Hunter" or "Falconer"

You’ll remember it from the film with the Frenchman up on the ramparts shouting down at Lancelot & King Arthur was they try and storm the castle (to very little effect).

You can visit this castle and, at least, enjoy the view from the coast. The castle is privately owned and there are a small number of tours offered each year. You can head to their [**official website for more info here.**](https://www.castlestalker.com/wp/)

[![Image 7: Castle Stalker in SCotland](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5efb46cf46fb3d2f36091afa/dd17ab4a-f176-4099-bd8a-75ca9b27bec3/Castle+Stalker.jpg)](https://www.scotlandswild.com/private-personalised-scotland-travel)

#### Doune Castle

The castle's impressive stone walls and turrets were used as the exterior of the _Castle of Guy de Lombard_, the villain in the film.

This historic castle was the setting for numerous unforgettable moments, including the scenes with the _French Taunters and the Wedding at Swamp Castle_—though fortunately, the castle has not sunk into a swamp!

In addition to Monty Python, Doune Castle has been featured in _Game of Thrones_ as Winterfell and in _Outlander_. The Great Hall, where the Knights of the Round Table sing and dance "when they're able," was also filmed inside the castle.

[![Image 8: The little white house in Glencoe](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5efb46cf46fb3d2f36091afa/466dd93d-2f35-4700-ba0f-24786abd0ccd/Glencoe.jpg)](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/glencoe-scottish-highlands-guided-group-1-day-tour-departing-glasgow)

#### Glencoe

With towering mountains on either side, Glen Coe provided the dramatic setting for the **Bridge of Death** near the film’s end. The glen has also been used in _Harry Potter_ films, serving as the backdrop for Hagrid’s Hut, the Forbidden Forest, and various outdoor shots of Hogwarts (although the castle itself is [**Alwick castle in England**](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/alnwick-castle-rosslyn-chapel-hogwarts-day-tour-from-edinburgh)).

Glen Coe is also **infamous for the 1692 massacre of Clan MacDonald**, who were killed by soldiers they had given hospitality to after failing to pledge allegiance to the new monarchs, William and Mary.

The scenic drive through Glen Coe follows the A82 and is probably the most stunning drive in the entire country - absolutely not to be missed. [**Take a day tour from Glasgow to Glencoe and see all the best bits.**](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/glencoe-scottish-highlands-guided-group-1-day-tour-departing-glasgow)

* * *

Monty Python and The Holy Grail is a beloved classic that continues to inspire and delight audiences today. Fans of the film can visit these iconic Scottish locations and many other filming locations throughout Scotland!

# Monty Python

## Monty Python and The Holy Grail Filming Locations in Scotland

Monty Python and The Holy Grail is a 1975 British comedy film that has become a cult classic over the years. The film is set in medieval England, but several of its **most memorable scenes were actually filmed in Scotland**.

The filmmakers chose Scotland because of its stunning landscapes and historic castles, which made the perfect backdrop in contract to the film's wacky characters and absurd humour.

**Fans of the film can still visit these locations and even recreate their favourite scenes.** In fact, you can join us on various tours around Scotland including a [**day tour to filming locations**](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/alnwick-castle-rosslyn-chapel-hogwarts-day-tour-from-edinburgh) (_Hogwarts from Harry Potter, New Asgard from the Avengers, Rosslyn Chapel from The Da Vinci Code and Leaderfoot Viaduct from Indiana Jones_).

Alternatively, [**check-out this day tour to Doune Castle**](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/outlander-doune-castle-loch-lomond-day-tour-from-glasgow) (_below: Castle of Guy de Lombar_) & more.

**Right, let’s jump into some of the locations from the film!**

[![Image 6: A stone castle viewed from a grassy landscape, surrounded by trees with leaves in the foreground.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5efb46cf46fb3d2f36091afa/4b260846-4294-4876-a614-1c9fcc49f6ca/Doune+Castle.jpg)](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/outlander-doune-castle-loch-lomond-day-tour-from-glasgow)

#### Castle Stalker

Name: From the Gaelic Word "Stalcaire" Meaning "Hunter" or "Falconer"

You’ll remember it from the film with the Frenchman up on the ramparts shouting down at Lancelot & King Arthur was they try and storm the castle (to very little effect).

You can visit this castle and, at least, enjoy the view from the coast. The castle is privately owned and there are a small number of tours offered each year. You can head to their [**official website for more info here.**](https://www.castlestalker.com/wp/)

[![Image 7: Castle Stalker in SCotland](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5efb46cf46fb3d2f36091afa/dd17ab4a-f176-4099-bd8a-75ca9b27bec3/Castle+Stalker.jpg)](https://www.scotlandswild.com/private-personalised-scotland-travel)

#### Doune Castle

The castle's impressive stone walls and turrets were used as the exterior of the _Castle of Guy de Lombard_, the villain in the film.

This historic castle was the setting for numerous unforgettable moments, including the scenes with the _French Taunters and the Wedding at Swamp Castle_—though fortunately, the castle has not sunk into a swamp!

In addition to Monty Python, Doune Castle has been featured in _Game of Thrones_ as Winterfell and in _Outlander_. The Great Hall, where the Knights of the Round Table sing and dance "when they're able," was also filmed inside the castle.

[![Image 8: The little white house in Glencoe](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5efb46cf46fb3d2f36091afa/466dd93d-2f35-4700-ba0f-24786abd0ccd/Glencoe.jpg)](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/glencoe-scottish-highlands-guided-group-1-day-tour-departing-glasgow)

#### Glencoe

With towering mountains on either side, Glen Coe provided the dramatic setting for the **Bridge of Death** near the film’s end. The glen has also been used in _Harry Potter_ films, serving as the backdrop for Hagrid’s Hut, the Forbidden Forest, and various outdoor shots of Hogwarts (although the castle itself is [**Alwick castle in England**](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/alnwick-castle-rosslyn-chapel-hogwarts-day-tour-from-edinburgh)).

Glen Coe is also **infamous for the 1692 massacre of Clan MacDonald**, who were killed by soldiers they had given hospitality to after failing to pledge allegiance to the new monarchs, William and Mary.

The scenic drive through Glen Coe follows the A82 and is probably the most stunning drive in the entire country - absolutely not to be missed. [**Take a day tour from Glasgow to Glencoe and see all the best bits.**](https://www.scotlandswild.com/our-scotland-group-tours/glencoe-scottish-highlands-guided-group-1-day-tour-departing-glasgow)

* * *

Monty Python and The Holy Grail is a beloved classic that continues to inspire and delight audiences today. Fans of the film can visit these iconic Scottish locations and many other filming locations throughout Scotland!

# Uncover Scotland’s Top Filming Locations with Highland Experience Tours

**Lights, Camera, Scotland!**

Scotland’s breath-taking landscapes have set the stage for some of the most iconic films and TV series. With Highland Experience Tours, you can step into the cinematic world and explore the very locations that have captured the hearts of audiences worldwide.

**Discover Iconic Filming Spots**

Join us on a journey to the stunning filming locations featured in popular movies and TV shows:

*   **Outlander**: Step into the world of [Outlander](https://www.highlandexperience.com/edinburgh-tours/outlander-experience/) as we visit the picturesque settings of this beloved series, including Doune Castle and Highland Folk Museum.
*   **Harry Potter**: Experience the magic of Harry Potter as we take you to the famous [Glenfinnan Viaduct](https://www.highlandexperience.com/edinburgh-tours/skye-the-jacobite-train/), and the majestic [Glencoe.](https://www.highlandexperience.com/edinburgh-tours/loch-ness-scottish-highlands/)
*   **Braveheart**: Visit the historic sites where the epic Braveheart was filmed, including the awe-inspiring [Glencoe](https://www.highlandexperience.com/glasgow-edinburgh/skye-tour/) and Glen Nevis.

**Chariots of Fire – West Sands Beach (St Andrews):**

The filming location of West Sands Beach in [St Andrews](https://www.highlandexperience.com/edinburgh-tours/st-andrews/) holds a significant place in cinematic history as the setting for the iconic opening scene of the award-winning film “Chariots of Fire.” This picturesque beach, situated adjacent to the renowned Old Course, provides the backdrop for the memorable slow-motion run featuring the film’s athletes. The visually stunning coastline, with its expansive stretch of golden sand and captivating sea views, sets the stage for one of the most famous moments in movie history. The combination of the athletes’ barefoot run and Vangelis’ evocative score against the backdrop of St Andrews’ natural beauty has etched West Sands Beach into the hearts of film enthusiasts and visitors alike, cementing its status as a cherished and enduring cinematic location.

**Highlander – Eilean Donan Castle:**

Eilean Donan Castle in Dornie served as the castle and village of Glenfinnan in the 1986 film “Highlander.” The picturesque castle also made an appearance in “The World is Not Enough” (1999) and “Made of Honour” (2008). Visitors can explore the castle’s role during the Jacobite risings, view historic artefacts, and even spot wildlife from the castle walls. The castle’s captivating setting and rich history make it a must-visit location for fans of these films.

[![Image 3: Eilean Donan Castle - a stunning castle to visit in Scotland](https://www.highlandexperience.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4610/2024/04/NewsletterLandspace-9.png?w=1000&h=1000)](https://www.highlandexperience.com/scotland-tours/)

**Skyfall – Glen Coe:**

Glen Coe, with its rugged peaks, played a prominent role in the 2012 James Bond film “Skyfall.” The striking Buachaille Etive Mor in Glen Coe provided the stunning backdrop for the secret agent’s Scottish home, Skyfall Lodge. The breathtaking Scottish setting added depth to the film’s captivating narrative, making it a memorable location for fans of the James Bond franchise.

**Game of Thrones – Doune:**

Doune Castle in Perthshire has had its fair share of stardom in both movies and TV shows. It was the set for multiple locations in “Monty Python and the Holy Grail” (1975) and served as the fictional Castle Leoch in “Outlander” (2014). Additionally, the castle was Winterfell in the pilot episode of “Game of Thrones” (2011). Visitors to Doune Castle can immerse themselves in the rich cinematic history and explore the castle’s on-screen legacy, making it a captivating destination for fans of these acclaimed productions.

**Outlaw King:**

The filming locations for the movie “Outlaw King” are diverse and include various historically significant and picturesque sites across Scotland. Some of the notable locations used for filming include:

1.   **Linlithgow Palace & St Michael’s Parish Church**: Linlithgow Palace and St Michael’s Parish Church served as filming locations for scenes related to Robert the Bruce and Elizabeth de Burgh’s wedding and the funeral for Robert’s father. These historical sites, rich in architectural and cultural significance, provided an authentic backdrop for key moments in the film.
2.   **Borthwick Castle**: Borthwick Castle, located in North Middleton, was used as a filming location for scenes depicting dramatic events, including the burning of the castle. The castle’s imposing structure and historical significance contributed to the visual authenticity of the film.
3.   **Doune Castle**: Doune Castle, known for its role in “Monty Python and the Holy Grail,” was utilized as a filming location for scenes involving the burning of the castle by the Lord of Douglas. The castle’s historical charm and medieval architecture added depth to the film’s portrayal of significant events.
4.   **Craigmillar Castle**: Craigmillar Castle, often referred to as Edinburgh’s “other castle,” was featured in the film as a stand-in for Bruce’s castle and village, as well as for Kildrummy Castle. The castle’s picturesque surroundings and historical relevance enhanced the film’s portrayal of key settings.
5.   **Dunfermline Abbey**: Scenes related to a significant historical event, such as the message delivery, were filmed at Dunfermline Abbey, specifically in The Nave, the oldest part of the Abbey. The abbey’s distinctive architecture and historical significance provided an authentic setting for pivotal scenes in the film.
6.   **Glasgow Cathedral**: The University of Glasgow Cloisters, part of Glasgow Cathedral, served as a filming location for scenes requiring a medieval banquet hall, adding an authentic historical ambiance to the film.
7.   **Muiravonside Country Park and Mugdock Country Park**: These natural settings were utilized as filming locations for specific scenes, including the depiction of the Battle of Loudoun Hill. The parks’ scenic beauty and expansive landscapes contributed to the visual grandeur of the film.
8.   **Aviemore and Isle of Skye (Talisker Bay, Coral Beaches, and Loch Dunvegan)**: Various stunning locations on the Isle of Skye, including Talisker Bay, Coral Beaches, and Loch Dunvegan, provided captivating backdrops for scenes pivotal to the film’s narrative.

These diverse filming locations, ranging from historical castles and churches to picturesque natural landscapes, played a crucial role in bringing the story of Robert the Bruce and the Scottish Wars of Independence to life in the movie “Outlaw King.”

[![Image 4: A gorgeous beach in Scotland](https://www.highlandexperience.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4610/2024/04/NewsletterLandspace-10.png?w=1000&h=1000)](https://www.highlandexperience.com/scotland-tours/)

**Experience Scotland’s Rich Film Heritage**

Immerse yourself in the captivating landscapes and rich history of Scotland as we delve into the film locations that have captured the imagination of audiences worldwide. Our award-winning local guides will bring these locations to life with their wealth of knowledge and passion for storytelling.

**Book Your Cinematic Adventure Today!**

Embark on a cinematic journey through Scotland’s most picturesque locations with Highland Experience Tours. Let us transport you to the enchanting world of film while experiencing the warmth of Highland hospitality. Book your tour today and create memories that will last a lifetime.

**Lights, camera, action – your Scottish adventure awaits!**

Contact us at 0131 226 1414 or email [info@highlandexperience.com](mailto:info@highlandexperience.com) to book your tour and embark on an unforgettable cinematic adventure with Highland Experience.

# Uncover Scotland’s Top Filming Locations with Highland Experience Tours

**Lights, Camera, Scotland!**

Scotland’s breath-taking landscapes have set the stage for some of the most iconic films and TV series. With Highland Experience Tours, you can step into the cinematic world and explore the very locations that have captured the hearts of audiences worldwide.

**Discover Iconic Filming Spots**

Join us on a journey to the stunning filming locations featured in popular movies and TV shows:

*   **Outlander**: Step into the world of [Outlander](https://www.highlandexperience.com/edinburgh-tours/outlander-experience/) as we visit the picturesque settings of this beloved series, including Doune Castle and Highland Folk Museum.
*   **Harry Potter**: Experience the magic of Harry Potter as we take you to the famous [Glenfinnan Viaduct](https://www.highlandexperience.com/edinburgh-tours/skye-the-jacobite-train/), and the majestic [Glencoe.](https://www.highlandexperience.com/edinburgh-tours/loch-ness-scottish-highlands/)
*   **Braveheart**: Visit the historic sites where the epic Braveheart was filmed, including the awe-inspiring [Glencoe](https://www.highlandexperience.com/glasgow-edinburgh/skye-tour/) and Glen Nevis.

**Chariots of Fire – West Sands Beach (St Andrews):**

The filming location of West Sands Beach in [St Andrews](https://www.highlandexperience.com/edinburgh-tours/st-andrews/) holds a significant place in cinematic history as the setting for the iconic opening scene of the award-winning film “Chariots of Fire.” This picturesque beach, situated adjacent to the renowned Old Course, provides the backdrop for the memorable slow-motion run featuring the film’s athletes. The visually stunning coastline, with its expansive stretch of golden sand and captivating sea views, sets the stage for one of the most famous moments in movie history. The combination of the athletes’ barefoot run and Vangelis’ evocative score against the backdrop of St Andrews’ natural beauty has etched West Sands Beach into the hearts of film enthusiasts and visitors alike, cementing its status as a cherished and enduring cinematic location.

**Highlander – Eilean Donan Castle:**

Eilean Donan Castle in Dornie served as the castle and village of Glenfinnan in the 1986 film “Highlander.” The picturesque castle also made an appearance in “The World is Not Enough” (1999) and “Made of Honour” (2008). Visitors can explore the castle’s role during the Jacobite risings, view historic artefacts, and even spot wildlife from the castle walls. The castle’s captivating setting and rich history make it a must-visit location for fans of these films.

[![Image 3: Eilean Donan Castle - a stunning castle to visit in Scotland](https://www.highlandexperience.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4610/2024/04/NewsletterLandspace-9.png?w=1000&h=1000)](https://www.highlandexperience.com/scotland-tours/)

**Skyfall – Glen Coe:**

Glen Coe, with its rugged peaks, played a prominent role in the 2012 James Bond film “Skyfall.” The striking Buachaille Etive Mor in Glen Coe provided the stunning backdrop for the secret agent’s Scottish home, Skyfall Lodge. The breathtaking Scottish setting added depth to the film’s captivating narrative, making it a memorable location for fans of the James Bond franchise.

**Game of Thrones – Doune:**

Doune Castle in Perthshire has had its fair share of stardom in both movies and TV shows. It was the set for multiple locations in “Monty Python and the Holy Grail” (1975) and served as the fictional Castle Leoch in “Outlander” (2014). Additionally, the castle was Winterfell in the pilot episode of “Game of Thrones” (2011). Visitors to Doune Castle can immerse themselves in the rich cinematic history and explore the castle’s on-screen legacy, making it a captivating destination for fans of these acclaimed productions.

**Outlaw King:**

The filming locations for the movie “Outlaw King” are diverse and include various historically significant and picturesque sites across Scotland. Some of the notable locations used for filming include:

1.   **Linlithgow Palace & St Michael’s Parish Church**: Linlithgow Palace and St Michael’s Parish Church served as filming locations for scenes related to Robert the Bruce and Elizabeth de Burgh’s wedding and the funeral for Robert’s father. These historical sites, rich in architectural and cultural significance, provided an authentic backdrop for key moments in the film.
2.   **Borthwick Castle**: Borthwick Castle, located in North Middleton, was used as a filming location for scenes depicting dramatic events, including the burning of the castle. The castle’s imposing structure and historical significance contributed to the visual authenticity of the film.
3.   **Doune Castle**: Doune Castle, known for its role in “Monty Python and the Holy Grail,” was utilized as a filming location for scenes involving the burning of the castle by the Lord of Douglas. The castle’s historical charm and medieval architecture added depth to the film’s portrayal of significant events.
4.   **Craigmillar Castle**: Craigmillar Castle, often referred to as Edinburgh’s “other castle,” was featured in the film as a stand-in for Bruce’s castle and village, as well as for Kildrummy Castle. The castle’s picturesque surroundings and historical relevance enhanced the film’s portrayal of key settings.
5.   **Dunfermline Abbey**: Scenes related to a significant historical event, such as the message delivery, were filmed at Dunfermline Abbey, specifically in The Nave, the oldest part of the Abbey. The abbey’s distinctive architecture and historical significance provided an authentic setting for pivotal scenes in the film.
6.   **Glasgow Cathedral**: The University of Glasgow Cloisters, part of Glasgow Cathedral, served as a filming location for scenes requiring a medieval banquet hall, adding an authentic historical ambiance to the film.
7.   **Muiravonside Country Park and Mugdock Country Park**: These natural settings were utilized as filming locations for specific scenes, including the depiction of the Battle of Loudoun Hill. The parks’ scenic beauty and expansive landscapes contributed to the visual grandeur of the film.
8.   **Aviemore and Isle of Skye (Talisker Bay, Coral Beaches, and Loch Dunvegan)**: Various stunning locations on the Isle of Skye, including Talisker Bay, Coral Beaches, and Loch Dunvegan, provided captivating backdrops for scenes pivotal to the film’s narrative.

These diverse filming locations, ranging from historical castles and churches to picturesque natural landscapes, played a crucial role in bringing the story of Robert the Bruce and the Scottish Wars of Independence to life in the movie “Outlaw King.”

**Tulliallan Castle** is a large house in [Kincardine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kincardine-on-Forth "Kincardine-on-Forth"), Fife, Scotland. It is the second structure to have the name, and is a mixture of [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") and Italian style architecture set amid some 90 acres (36 hectares) of parkland just north of where the [Kincardine Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kincardine_Bridge "Kincardine Bridge") spans the [Firth of Forth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firth_of_Forth "Firth of Forth").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan_Castle#cite_note-:0-1) It has been the home of the [Scottish Police College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Police_College "Scottish Police College") since 1954. On 1 April 2013, Tulliallan Castle became the headquarters of [Police Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_Scotland "Police Scotland") (the newly created national police service for Scotland), but in 2014 the service's headquarters temporarily relocated to nearby [Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling "Stirling") in the former Central Scotland Police HQ.

## 14th-century castle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: 14th-century castle")]

An earlier structure about 1⁄2 mile (800 metres) northwest, [Old Tulliallan Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Tulliallan_Castle "Old Tulliallan Castle"), was built by 1304, when it was ordered to be strengthened by [Edward I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I "Edward I") of England, it then passed into the ownership of [William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Douglas,_1st_Earl_of_Douglas "William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas"), and was granted by the Douglases to the Edmonstones, and thence to a junior branch of the [Blackadders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Blackadder "Clan Blackadder"), and finally to the [Bruces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Bruce "Clan Bruce") of Carnock. A [fortified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortified "Fortified") house with a [keep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep "Keep") and [rib-vaulted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rib_vault "Rib vault") ground floor, it was abandoned in the seventeenth century.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan_Castle#cite_note-2)

## 19th-century castle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 19th-century castle")]

The castle was built in 1812–1820 for Admiral [Lord Keith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Elphinstone,_1st_Viscount_Keith "George Elphinstone, 1st Viscount Keith"), one time senior officer of [Lord Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Nelson "Lord Nelson"), paid for with [prize money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prize_money "Prize money"). The labour force said to include French prisoners of war.

During the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") it was used by the [Polish Armed Forces in the West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Armed_Forces_in_the_West "Polish Armed Forces in the West") as their headquarters in Scotland.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan_Castle#cite_note-:0-1)

Prior to the Second World War there was no central training for police officers in Scotland. After the war it was decided to centralise all police training and Tulliallan was the result. Tulliallan, from the Gaelic _Tulach-Aluin_ ('beautiful knoll') was purchased in 1950 by the then [Scottish Home Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Home_Department "Scottish Home Department") for £9,100. The building was modernised and renovated and the first courses for inspectors and sergeants began in 1954. Over the years the site has been heavily modified to provide accommodation, catering, training, and teaching facilities for the [Scottish Police College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Police_College "Scottish Police College").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan_Castle#cite_note-3)

The building is now used as the administrative head of the Scottish Police College and also serves as the official residence of the Chief Constable of [Police Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_Scotland "Police Scotland").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan_Castle#cite_note-4)

The building is sometimes colloquially known as "Castle Grayskull" by serving and retired officers in relation to the castle in the [He Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He-Man_and_the_Masters_of_the_Universe "He-Man and the Masters of the Universe") fictional series.

**Tulliallan Castle** is a large house in [Kincardine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kincardine-on-Forth "Kincardine-on-Forth"), Fife, Scotland. It is the second structure to have the name, and is a mixture of [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") and Italian style architecture set amid some 90 acres (36 hectares) of parkland just north of where the [Kincardine Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kincardine_Bridge "Kincardine Bridge") spans the [Firth of Forth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firth_of_Forth "Firth of Forth").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan_Castle#cite_note-:0-1) It has been the home of the [Scottish Police College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Police_College "Scottish Police College") since 1954. On 1 April 2013, Tulliallan Castle became the headquarters of [Police Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_Scotland "Police Scotland") (the newly created national police service for Scotland), but in 2014 the service's headquarters temporarily relocated to nearby [Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling "Stirling") in the former Central Scotland Police HQ.

## 14th-century castle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: 14th-century castle")]

An earlier structure about 1⁄2 mile (800 metres) northwest, [Old Tulliallan Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Tulliallan_Castle "Old Tulliallan Castle"), was built by 1304, when it was ordered to be strengthened by [Edward I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I "Edward I") of England, it then passed into the ownership of [William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Douglas,_1st_Earl_of_Douglas "William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas"), and was granted by the Douglases to the Edmonstones, and thence to a junior branch of the [Blackadders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Blackadder "Clan Blackadder"), and finally to the [Bruces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Bruce "Clan Bruce") of Carnock. A [fortified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortified "Fortified") house with a [keep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep "Keep") and [rib-vaulted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rib_vault "Rib vault") ground floor, it was abandoned in the seventeenth century.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan_Castle#cite_note-2)

## 19th-century castle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 19th-century castle")]

The castle was built in 1812–1820 for Admiral [Lord Keith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Elphinstone,_1st_Viscount_Keith "George Elphinstone, 1st Viscount Keith"), one time senior officer of [Lord Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Nelson "Lord Nelson"), paid for with [prize money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prize_money "Prize money"). The labour force said to include French prisoners of war.

During the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") it was used by the [Polish Armed Forces in the West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Armed_Forces_in_the_West "Polish Armed Forces in the West") as their headquarters in Scotland.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan_Castle#cite_note-:0-1)

Prior to the Second World War there was no central training for police officers in Scotland. After the war it was decided to centralise all police training and Tulliallan was the result. Tulliallan, from the Gaelic _Tulach-Aluin_ ('beautiful knoll') was purchased in 1950 by the then [Scottish Home Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Home_Department "Scottish Home Department") for £9,100. The building was modernised and renovated and the first courses for inspectors and sergeants began in 1954. Over the years the site has been heavily modified to provide accommodation, catering, training, and teaching facilities for the [Scottish Police College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Police_College "Scottish Police College").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan_Castle#cite_note-3)

The building is now used as the administrative head of the Scottish Police College and also serves as the official residence of the Chief Constable of [Police Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_Scotland "Police Scotland").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan_Castle#cite_note-4)

The building is sometimes colloquially known as "Castle Grayskull" by serving and retired officers in relation to the castle in the [He Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He-Man_and_the_Masters_of_the_Universe "He-Man and the Masters of the Universe") fictional series.

Just 11 miles west of Dunfermline,

Tulliallan is far more than Scotland’s police college.

Set in magnificent parkland near Kincardine, the early-19th-century Tulliallan Castle has lived several remarkable lives: a grand estate built for Admiral Lord Keith, wartime headquarters of the Polish Armed Forces in Scotland, and—since the 1950s—the home of the Scottish Police College.

Its grounds are a story in themselves. Historic Environment Scotland notes Tulliallan’s impressive collection of specimen conifers and distinctive deciduous trees, planted to frame the castle, shelter the estate and create sweeping views towards the Forth. These mature trees are living links to the landscape ambitions of the nineteenth-century estate.

A place of policing, Polish-Scottish wartime history, architecture and remarkable trees—Tulliallan remains one of the area’s most fascinating historic landscapes.

You can also access Devilla Forest from the grounds so it is a fantastic place to walk.

Just 11 miles west of Dunfermline,

Tulliallan is far more than Scotland’s police college.

Set in magnificent parkland near Kincardine, the early-19th-century Tulliallan Castle has lived several remarkable lives: a grand estate built for Admiral Lord Keith, wartime headquarters of the Polish Armed Forces in Scotland, and—since the 1950s—the home of the Scottish Police College.

Its grounds are a story in themselves. Historic Environment Scotland notes Tulliallan’s impressive collection of specimen conifers and distinctive deciduous trees, planted to frame the castle, shelter the estate and create sweeping views towards the Forth. These mature trees are living links to the landscape ambitions of the nineteenth-century estate.

A place of policing, Polish-Scottish wartime history, architecture and remarkable trees—Tulliallan remains one of the area’s most fascinating historic landscapes.

You can also access Devilla Forest from the grounds so it is a fantastic place to walk.

**Tulliallan** (Gaelic _Tulach Àlainn_, 'Beautiful knoll') was an estate in [Perthshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perthshire "Perthshire"), Scotland, near to [Kincardine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kincardine-on-Forth "Kincardine-on-Forth"), and a [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_parishes_in_Scotland "Civil parishes in Scotland"). The [Blackadder lairds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Blackadder "Clan Blackadder") of Tulliallan, a branch of the Blackadder border clan, wielded considerable power in the 15th and 16th centuries. The modern Tulliallan Castle is relatively recent, built in 1812–1820 and now the home of the [Scottish Police College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Police_College "Scottish Police College").

## Parish

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Parish")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Felled_and_replanted_area%2C_Devilla_Forest_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1358282.jpg/250px-Felled_and_replanted_area%2C_Devilla_Forest_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1358282.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Felled_and_replanted_area,_Devilla_Forest_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1358282.jpg)

Felled and replanted area, Devilla Forest Known as Tulliallan Forest on older maps, Devilla is a long established forest on undulating, sometimes marshy ground.

The original parish of Tulliallan covered only the barony of Tulliallan. In 1673 it was extended to include the barony of [Kincardine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kincardine-on-Forth "Kincardine-on-Forth") and the lands of Lurg, Sands and Kellywood, formerly included in the neighbouring [Culross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culross "Culross") parish. For many years the parishes of Culross and Tulliallan formed an exclave some miles away from the rest of [Perthshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perthshire "Perthshire"), on the boundaries of [Clackmannanshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clackmannanshire "Clackmannanshire") and [Fife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fife "Fife").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGroome1885453-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-2) Culross and Tulliallan were transferred to Fife based on the recommendations of the boundary commission appointed under the [Local Government (Scotland) Act 1889](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Government_(Scotland)_Act_1889 "Local Government (Scotland) Act 1889").

The parish is bounded on the west and north by [Clackmannan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clackmannan "Clackmannan"), on the east by Culross and on the south by the [River Forth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Forth "River Forth"). It is 3.75 miles (6.04 km) from north to south and 3 miles (4.8 km) from east to west, and contains 4,176 acres (1,690 ha). In 1885, 484 acres (196 ha) were foreshore and 106 acres (43 ha) water. The parish slopes gently southward to the Forth from a height of 324 feet (99 m). Between 1823 and 1839 a large area of land was recovered from the tidal waters of the Forth by two large embankments. The 1885 description said about 500 acres (200 ha) was wooded and almost all the rest cultivated. High-quality sandstone had been quarried near Longannet for many years. The land was also rich in coal and ironstone.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGroome1885453-1)

At the last census (2011), the population of the civil parish was 3,001.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-cen2011-3) The area of the parish is 3,685 acres.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-4) Tulliallan parish is also a Community Council area under the name Kincardine, with some variations in the boundary with [Culross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culross "Culross"), its neighbouring civil parish and community council to the east.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-5)

## Old castle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Old castle")]

The first fortification at Tulliallan was built some time before 1304, when it was ordered to be strengthened by [Edward I of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I_of_England "Edward I of England"). The position was strategic, near the main ferry over the Forth, and in 1304 Edward I gave orders for the walls of "Tolyalwyn" to be strengthened. Presumably this would have included strengthening the D-shaped moat and the outer rampart, making the position strong against attack across the marshy land, which would not be drained until the 18th century. There would have been buildings within the enclosure, but the old castle was probably built later, by the Douglasses.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGifford1988268-6)

The Douglas castle was initially an L-shaped two-storey building of ashlar masonry, with a tower at the southwest corner holding the main entrance, which was reached by a drawbridge. Most of the ground floor had small, square windows, while there were large slits above. The interior was unusual in that there were important rooms on the ground floor. The ceilings of these rooms included ribbed vaults springing from octagonal piers. The house was extended in the fifteenth century, and a major reconstruction seems to have been undertaken in the late sixteenth century.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGifford1988268%E2%80%93269-7)

The castle was surrounded by a moat, which would have been filled by water from the [Firth of Forth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firth_of_Forth "Firth of Forth"), which in the old days extended further inland. An 1853 account of the then-ruined building said "two narrow posterns open from each end of the southern front, of which that on the east opens into an apartment which has been termed the great hall, where three compartments are curiously formed by elegant groined arches, which rest upon a central octagonal column, the whole being in a state of remarkable preservation. [[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1853209-8) In 1885 the old castle, although ruined, was still described as an imposing-looking edifice.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeveridgeDalgleish188522-9)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")]

The castle passed into the ownership of [William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Douglas,_1st_Earl_of_Douglas "William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas") (c. 1327–1384). [Archibald Douglas, 4th Earl of Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Douglas,_4th_Earl_of_Douglas "Archibald Douglas, 4th Earl of Douglas") gifted the Tulliallan estate to the Edmiston family in 1402. In 1456 the gift was confirmed to Sir James Edmiston, great-grandson of King [Robert II of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_II_of_Scotland "Robert II of Scotland"), by royal charter. Patrick Blackader, grandson of Cuthbert Blackader of [Blackader Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackader_Castle "Blackader Castle") in [Berwickshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berwickshire "Berwickshire"), married Elizabeth Edmiston, daughter of Sir James. She brought the Tulliallan estate as her dowry.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTELothian186270-10)

A noted member of the Blackadder family of Tulliallan was [Robert Blackadder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Blackadder "Robert Blackadder"), brother of Patrick Blackadder, Laird of Tulliallan.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeveridgeDalgleish188590-11) Robert Blackadder was Bishop of Aberdeen, Bishop of Glasgow from 1484 and then in 1492 the first [Archbishop of Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Glasgow "Archbishop of Glasgow"), who added the eponymous crypt and aisle in [Glasgow Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow_Cathedral "Glasgow Cathedral"). The bishop sided with rebel nobles who defeated and killed King [James III of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_III_of_Scotland "James III of Scotland") in 1488 at the [Battle of Sauchieburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sauchieburn "Battle of Sauchieburn"). The archbishop died while on a [pilgrimage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilgrimage "Pilgrimage") to the [Holy Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Land "Holy Land") in 1508.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTESeal_and_brief_history...-12)

One of the Lairds of Tulliallan, Sir John Blackadder, was beheaded in March 1531 for the murder of James Inglis, [Abbot of Culross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbot_of_Culross "Abbot of Culross"), in a dispute over land.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeveridgeDalgleish188594%E2%80%9395-13) He was succeeded at Tulliallan by his brother Patrick, who renewed a dispute against the Homes for the Blackadder family lands around [Allanton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allanton,_Scottish_Borders "Allanton, Scottish Borders") in [Berwickshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berwickshire "Berwickshire"). Patrick was murdered in an ambush near Edinburgh, where he was to meet the Homes to try to resolve their differences. Following this the Blackadders made no further attempts to recover their ancestral estates.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson1877309-14) William Blackadder was among the supporters of [Mary, Queen of Scots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary,_Queen_of_Scots "Mary, Queen of Scots") at the [Battle of Carberry Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Carberry_Hill "Battle of Carberry Hill") (15 June 1567). He was arrested soon after and hanged in June, and his brother was hanged in September.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacRobert200213-15)

The last Blackadder to own Tulliallan was Sir John, born in 1596 and on 18 July 1626 created a knight baronet of Nova Scotia by King [Charles I of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"). His estate, with lime works, salt pans and other enterprises, yielded an income of 36,000 merks annually, but this was not enough to satisfy Sir John's expensive habits and he ran up debts far beyond his ability to pay. When his effects were seized he fled to the continent, and in 1642 seems to have been in the French service. He died in America in 1651. Sir John's wife, Elizabeth Graham, was the daughter of the [Earl of Menteith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Menteith "Earl of Menteith"). She had an annuity of 360 merks, and lived at Tulliallan until 1662. His son, Alexander, could not free the estate from the burden of debts that his father had contracted. The Court of Session ordered a judicial sale. In 1700 the estate was purchased by Colonel John Erskine, son of [David Erskine, 4th Lord Cardross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Erskine,_4th_Lord_Cardross?action=edit&redlink=1 "David Erskine, 4th Lord Cardross (page does not exist)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTELothian186270-10)

The celebrated covenanting preacher [John Blackadder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Blackadder_(preacher) "John Blackadder (preacher)") (1622-1685) was legally the heir to the [Blackadder baronetcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackadder_baronets "Blackadder baronets"), but did not claim the title.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTENotes_and_Queries_188350-16)

## Later years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Later years")]

The last occupant of the old castle was Colonel Erskine, known locally as the "Black Colonel", who died in the 1790s. [George Elphinstone, 1st Viscount Keith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Elphinstone,_1st_Viscount_Keith "George Elphinstone, 1st Viscount Keith") bought the estate in 1799, and built today's castle as his family residence.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1853210-17) The roof of the old castle was removed and it was allowed to crumble into ruins.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTELothian186270-10) An ancient bronze kettle was dug out of these ruins, about 8.5 inches (22 cm) in diameter and 5 inches (13 cm) high. Legend says that it formerly hung from one of the bosses of the castle roof, filled with gold. As long as it hung there, the castle would stand and the Blackadders of Tulliallan would prosper.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1853209-8)

The modern-day Tulliallan Castle is about a half mile to the southeast of the old castle, built in 1818-1820 for Lord Viscount Keith. The building was acquired by the Mitchell family in 1924. During the [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") it was the headquarters of the [Polish Armed Forces in the West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Armed_Forces_in_the_West "Polish Armed Forces in the West"). It has been the home of the [Scottish Police College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Police_College "Scottish Police College") since 1954 and was the temporary headquarters of [Police Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_Scotland "Police Scotland") upon its creation in 2013.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTETulliallan_Castle-18)

**Tulliallan** (Gaelic _Tulach Àlainn_, 'Beautiful knoll') was an estate in [Perthshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perthshire "Perthshire"), Scotland, near to [Kincardine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kincardine-on-Forth "Kincardine-on-Forth"), and a [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_parishes_in_Scotland "Civil parishes in Scotland"). The [Blackadder lairds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Blackadder "Clan Blackadder") of Tulliallan, a branch of the Blackadder border clan, wielded considerable power in the 15th and 16th centuries. The modern Tulliallan Castle is relatively recent, built in 1812–1820 and now the home of the [Scottish Police College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Police_College "Scottish Police College").

## Parish

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Parish")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Felled_and_replanted_area%2C_Devilla_Forest_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1358282.jpg/250px-Felled_and_replanted_area%2C_Devilla_Forest_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1358282.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Felled_and_replanted_area,_Devilla_Forest_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1358282.jpg)

Felled and replanted area, Devilla Forest Known as Tulliallan Forest on older maps, Devilla is a long established forest on undulating, sometimes marshy ground.

The original parish of Tulliallan covered only the barony of Tulliallan. In 1673 it was extended to include the barony of [Kincardine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kincardine-on-Forth "Kincardine-on-Forth") and the lands of Lurg, Sands and Kellywood, formerly included in the neighbouring [Culross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culross "Culross") parish. For many years the parishes of Culross and Tulliallan formed an exclave some miles away from the rest of [Perthshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perthshire "Perthshire"), on the boundaries of [Clackmannanshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clackmannanshire "Clackmannanshire") and [Fife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fife "Fife").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGroome1885453-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-2) Culross and Tulliallan were transferred to Fife based on the recommendations of the boundary commission appointed under the [Local Government (Scotland) Act 1889](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Government_(Scotland)_Act_1889 "Local Government (Scotland) Act 1889").

The parish is bounded on the west and north by [Clackmannan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clackmannan "Clackmannan"), on the east by Culross and on the south by the [River Forth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Forth "River Forth"). It is 3.75 miles (6.04 km) from north to south and 3 miles (4.8 km) from east to west, and contains 4,176 acres (1,690 ha). In 1885, 484 acres (196 ha) were foreshore and 106 acres (43 ha) water. The parish slopes gently southward to the Forth from a height of 324 feet (99 m). Between 1823 and 1839 a large area of land was recovered from the tidal waters of the Forth by two large embankments. The 1885 description said about 500 acres (200 ha) was wooded and almost all the rest cultivated. High-quality sandstone had been quarried near Longannet for many years. The land was also rich in coal and ironstone.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGroome1885453-1)

At the last census (2011), the population of the civil parish was 3,001.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-cen2011-3) The area of the parish is 3,685 acres.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-4) Tulliallan parish is also a Community Council area under the name Kincardine, with some variations in the boundary with [Culross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culross "Culross"), its neighbouring civil parish and community council to the east.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-5)

## Old castle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Old castle")]

The first fortification at Tulliallan was built some time before 1304, when it was ordered to be strengthened by [Edward I of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I_of_England "Edward I of England"). The position was strategic, near the main ferry over the Forth, and in 1304 Edward I gave orders for the walls of "Tolyalwyn" to be strengthened. Presumably this would have included strengthening the D-shaped moat and the outer rampart, making the position strong against attack across the marshy land, which would not be drained until the 18th century. There would have been buildings within the enclosure, but the old castle was probably built later, by the Douglasses.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGifford1988268-6)

The Douglas castle was initially an L-shaped two-storey building of ashlar masonry, with a tower at the southwest corner holding the main entrance, which was reached by a drawbridge. Most of the ground floor had small, square windows, while there were large slits above. The interior was unusual in that there were important rooms on the ground floor. The ceilings of these rooms included ribbed vaults springing from octagonal piers. The house was extended in the fifteenth century, and a major reconstruction seems to have been undertaken in the late sixteenth century.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGifford1988268%E2%80%93269-7)

The castle was surrounded by a moat, which would have been filled by water from the [Firth of Forth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firth_of_Forth "Firth of Forth"), which in the old days extended further inland. An 1853 account of the then-ruined building said "two narrow posterns open from each end of the southern front, of which that on the east opens into an apartment which has been termed the great hall, where three compartments are curiously formed by elegant groined arches, which rest upon a central octagonal column, the whole being in a state of remarkable preservation. [[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1853209-8) In 1885 the old castle, although ruined, was still described as an imposing-looking edifice.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeveridgeDalgleish188522-9)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")]

The castle passed into the ownership of [William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Douglas,_1st_Earl_of_Douglas "William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas") (c. 1327–1384). [Archibald Douglas, 4th Earl of Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Douglas,_4th_Earl_of_Douglas "Archibald Douglas, 4th Earl of Douglas") gifted the Tulliallan estate to the Edmiston family in 1402. In 1456 the gift was confirmed to Sir James Edmiston, great-grandson of King [Robert II of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_II_of_Scotland "Robert II of Scotland"), by royal charter. Patrick Blackader, grandson of Cuthbert Blackader of [Blackader Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackader_Castle "Blackader Castle") in [Berwickshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berwickshire "Berwickshire"), married Elizabeth Edmiston, daughter of Sir James. She brought the Tulliallan estate as her dowry.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTELothian186270-10)

A noted member of the Blackadder family of Tulliallan was [Robert Blackadder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Blackadder "Robert Blackadder"), brother of Patrick Blackadder, Laird of Tulliallan.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeveridgeDalgleish188590-11) Robert Blackadder was Bishop of Aberdeen, Bishop of Glasgow from 1484 and then in 1492 the first [Archbishop of Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Glasgow "Archbishop of Glasgow"), who added the eponymous crypt and aisle in [Glasgow Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow_Cathedral "Glasgow Cathedral"). The bishop sided with rebel nobles who defeated and killed King [James III of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_III_of_Scotland "James III of Scotland") in 1488 at the [Battle of Sauchieburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sauchieburn "Battle of Sauchieburn"). The archbishop died while on a [pilgrimage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilgrimage "Pilgrimage") to the [Holy Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Land "Holy Land") in 1508.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTESeal_and_brief_history...-12)

One of the Lairds of Tulliallan, Sir John Blackadder, was beheaded in March 1531 for the murder of James Inglis, [Abbot of Culross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbot_of_Culross "Abbot of Culross"), in a dispute over land.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeveridgeDalgleish188594%E2%80%9395-13) He was succeeded at Tulliallan by his brother Patrick, who renewed a dispute against the Homes for the Blackadder family lands around [Allanton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allanton,_Scottish_Borders "Allanton, Scottish Borders") in [Berwickshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berwickshire "Berwickshire"). Patrick was murdered in an ambush near Edinburgh, where he was to meet the Homes to try to resolve their differences. Following this the Blackadders made no further attempts to recover their ancestral estates.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson1877309-14) William Blackadder was among the supporters of [Mary, Queen of Scots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary,_Queen_of_Scots "Mary, Queen of Scots") at the [Battle of Carberry Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Carberry_Hill "Battle of Carberry Hill") (15 June 1567). He was arrested soon after and hanged in June, and his brother was hanged in September.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacRobert200213-15)

The last Blackadder to own Tulliallan was Sir John, born in 1596 and on 18 July 1626 created a knight baronet of Nova Scotia by King [Charles I of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"). His estate, with lime works, salt pans and other enterprises, yielded an income of 36,000 merks annually, but this was not enough to satisfy Sir John's expensive habits and he ran up debts far beyond his ability to pay. When his effects were seized he fled to the continent, and in 1642 seems to have been in the French service. He died in America in 1651. Sir John's wife, Elizabeth Graham, was the daughter of the [Earl of Menteith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Menteith "Earl of Menteith"). She had an annuity of 360 merks, and lived at Tulliallan until 1662. His son, Alexander, could not free the estate from the burden of debts that his father had contracted. The Court of Session ordered a judicial sale. In 1700 the estate was purchased by Colonel John Erskine, son of [David Erskine, 4th Lord Cardross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Erskine,_4th_Lord_Cardross?action=edit&redlink=1 "David Erskine, 4th Lord Cardross (page does not exist)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTELothian186270-10)

The celebrated covenanting preacher [John Blackadder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Blackadder_(preacher) "John Blackadder (preacher)") (1622-1685) was legally the heir to the [Blackadder baronetcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackadder_baronets "Blackadder baronets"), but did not claim the title.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTENotes_and_Queries_188350-16)

## Later years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tulliallan&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Later years")]

The last occupant of the old castle was Colonel Erskine, known locally as the "Black Colonel", who died in the 1790s. [George Elphinstone, 1st Viscount Keith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Elphinstone,_1st_Viscount_Keith "George Elphinstone, 1st Viscount Keith") bought the estate in 1799, and built today's castle as his family residence.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1853210-17) The roof of the old castle was removed and it was allowed to crumble into ruins.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTELothian186270-10) An ancient bronze kettle was dug out of these ruins, about 8.5 inches (22 cm) in diameter and 5 inches (13 cm) high. Legend says that it formerly hung from one of the bosses of the castle roof, filled with gold. As long as it hung there, the castle would stand and the Blackadders of Tulliallan would prosper.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1853209-8)

The modern-day Tulliallan Castle is about a half mile to the southeast of the old castle, built in 1818-1820 for Lord Viscount Keith. The building was acquired by the Mitchell family in 1924. During the [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") it was the headquarters of the [Polish Armed Forces in the West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Armed_Forces_in_the_West "Polish Armed Forces in the West"). It has been the home of the [Scottish Police College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Police_College "Scottish Police College") since 1954 and was the temporary headquarters of [Police Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_Scotland "Police Scotland") upon its creation in 2013.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulliallan#cite_note-FOOTNOTETulliallan_Castle-18)

Walking through he grounds of Tulliallan Castle which is now the Police Scotland collage where I spoke with a groundsman who working beside the Police memorial where he chatted about its history and pointed out the two tree planted by the Polish President and Prime Minister in 1941 whilst they were in exile and how it was used as the Polish Headquarters for Scotland which I posted earlier which also got us chatting about the terrible invasion of Ukraine ![Image 1: 🇺🇦](https://static.xx.fbcdn.net/images/emoji.php/v9/tf2/1/16/1f1fa_1f1e6.png). I then wandered down to Woodlea old cemetery which was closed so had to look over the wall. The gatehouse gates are magnificent with their thistle designs. Sad it’s not being looked after and being allowed to fall into disrepair and those imposing no entry signs ![Image 2: 😆](https://static.xx.fbcdn.net/images/emoji.php/v9/td4/1/16/1f606.png)

Tulliallan Castle is a large house in Kincardine, Fife. It is the second structure to have the name, and is a mixture of Gothic and Italian style architecture set amid some 90 acres (36 hectares) of parkland just north of where the Kincardine Bridge spans the Firth of Forth. It has been the home of the Scottish Police College since 1954. On 1 April 2013, Tulliallan Castle became the headquarters of Police Scotland (the newly created national police service for Scotland), but in 2014 the service's headquarters temporarily relocated to nearby Stirling in the former Central Scotland Police HQ.

14th-century castle - An earlier structure about 1⁄2 mile (800 metres) northwest, Old Tulliallan Castle, was built by 1304, when it was ordered to be strengthened by Edward I of England, it then passed into the ownership of William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas, and was granted by the Douglases to the Edmonstones, and thence to a junior branch of the Blackadders, and finally to the Bruces of Carnock. A fortified house with a keep and rib-vaulted ground floor, it was abandoned in the seventeenth century.

19th-century castle - The castle was built in 1812–1820 for Admiral Lord Keith, one time senior officer of Lord Nelson, from money received from prize ships. The labour force said to include French prisoners of war.

During the Second World War it was used by the Polish Armed Forces in the West as their headquarters in Scotland.

Prior to the Second World War there was no central training for police officers in Scotland. After the war it was decided to centralise all police training and Tulliallan was the result. Tulliallan, from the Gaelic Tulach-Aluin ('beautiful knoll') was purchased in 1950 by the then Scottish Home Department for £9,100. The building was modernised and renovated and the first courses for inspectors and sergeants began in 1954. Over the years the site has been heavily modified to provide accommodation, catering, training, and teaching facilities for the Scottish Police College.

The building is now used as the administrative head of the Scottish Police College and also serves as the official residence of the Chief Constable of Police Scotland.

A visit to Tulliallan today with the boys

Walking through he grounds of Tulliallan Castle which is now the Police Scotland collage where I spoke with a groundsman who working beside the Police memorial where he chatted about its history and pointed out the two tree planted by the Polish President and Prime Minister in 1941 whilst they were in exile and how it was used as the Polish Headquarters for Scotland which I posted earlier which also got us chatting about the terrible invasion of Ukraine ![Image 1: 🇺🇦](https://static.xx.fbcdn.net/images/emoji.php/v9/tf2/1/16/1f1fa_1f1e6.png). I then wandered down to Woodlea old cemetery which was closed so had to look over the wall. The gatehouse gates are magnificent with their thistle designs. Sad it’s not being looked after and being allowed to fall into disrepair and those imposing no entry signs ![Image 2: 😆](https://static.xx.fbcdn.net/images/emoji.php/v9/td4/1/16/1f606.png)

Tulliallan Castle is a large house in Kincardine, Fife. It is the second structure to have the name, and is a mixture of Gothic and Italian style architecture set amid some 90 acres (36 hectares) of parkland just north of where the Kincardine Bridge spans the Firth of Forth. It has been the home of the Scottish Police College since 1954. On 1 April 2013, Tulliallan Castle became the headquarters of Police Scotland (the newly created national police service for Scotland), but in 2014 the service's headquarters temporarily relocated to nearby Stirling in the former Central Scotland Police HQ.

14th-century castle - An earlier structure about 1⁄2 mile (800 metres) northwest, Old Tulliallan Castle, was built by 1304, when it was ordered to be strengthened by Edward I of England, it then passed into the ownership of William Douglas, 1st Earl of Douglas, and was granted by the Douglases to the Edmonstones, and thence to a junior branch of the Blackadders, and finally to the Bruces of Carnock. A fortified house with a keep and rib-vaulted ground floor, it was abandoned in the seventeenth century.

19th-century castle - The castle was built in 1812–1820 for Admiral Lord Keith, one time senior officer of Lord Nelson, from money received from prize ships. The labour force said to include French prisoners of war.

During the Second World War it was used by the Polish Armed Forces in the West as their headquarters in Scotland.

Prior to the Second World War there was no central training for police officers in Scotland. After the war it was decided to centralise all police training and Tulliallan was the result. Tulliallan, from the Gaelic Tulach-Aluin ('beautiful knoll') was purchased in 1950 by the then Scottish Home Department for £9,100. The building was modernised and renovated and the first courses for inspectors and sergeants began in 1954. Over the years the site has been heavily modified to provide accommodation, catering, training, and teaching facilities for the Scottish Police College.

The building is now used as the administrative head of the Scottish Police College and also serves as the official residence of the Chief Constable of Police Scotland.

TOWARDS THE END of the 18th century George Keith Elphinstone

Elphinstone, who later became Admiral Lord Keith, fought in

the Napoleonic wars.He was Admiral Lord Nelson's senior and

took the surrender of Napoleon on H.M.S. Bellerophon. During

the period 1815-1820 he built Tullyallan Castle (Gaelic Tulach-

gardens and picturesque plantations. The Castle was finished in

1820 but its beauty has been largely added to by his trustees and

successors." The Scottish Police College has benefited accordingly

from a century and a half of development.
